title: A Five-Dimensional Integrated Management Framework (ABCDE-F) for Critically Ill Patients with Obesity: A Hypothesis
content: Critically ill patients with obesity represent a clinically distinct population in whom respiratory mechanics, drug disposition, hemodynamic assessment, nutrition, positioning, and functional recovery are substantially influenced by excess adiposity and altered body composition. Existing evidence provides obesity-specific recommendations for individual domains—particularly airway management, mechanical ventilation, nutrition, positioning, and rehabilitation—but these recommendations are usually implemented as separate interventions rather than as a coordinated, whole-course management system. We therefore propose the ABCDE-F framework, a five-dimensional integrated management model in which A denotes Analgesia and Sedation, B Body Position, C Circulation and Perfusion, D Diet and Nutrition, and E Early Mobilization. F, Failure of Respiration, is not an additional parallel treatment dimension; rather, it is the central clinical anchor around which the five dimensions are organized. The framework is designed to follow the patient across the entire critical-care trajectory, from pre-intubation risk assessment through mechanical ventilation, weaning, extubation, post-extubation support, and transition to the ward. The hypothesis is that such integration may improve the consistency and timeliness of obesity-specific care, reduce avoidable variation between clinicians and shifts, facilitate ventilator liberation and recovery, and ultimately improve patient-centered outcomes. Our department has translated this concept into a standardized pathway incorporating an obesity critical care team, structured multidisciplinary rounds, daily F-ABCDE checklists, standardized weaning and transfer processes, and early post-ICU follow-up. A prospective clinical study is ongoing; interim observations are encouraging but are not presented here as efficacy evidence because the study has not yet completed and the results have not undergone peer review. This article presents the framework as a testable clinical hypothesis and defines a research agenda for prospective and multicenter validation.
